working_title: Hotels Pay 30% to Book Their Own Rooms
title_options: Hotels Pay 30% to Book Their Own Rooms
thumbnail_concepts: Split-frame: left side a warm-lit hotel front desk at night with no queue; right side a stark bar chart draining from 'booked' down to 'kept,' with the commission percentage as a bold overlay number.
Overhead shot of a hotel key-card rack — one lit card labeled 'Direct' surrounded by dim cards stamped with generic OTA-style logos, evoking how rare a direct booking actually is.
description_draft:
Independent hotels lose about two thirds of their bookings to Booking.com and Expedia, paying 18–30% in all-in commission once loyalty programs like Genius and Accelerator are added (Cloudbeds, 2026 State of Independent Hotels, ~90M bookings analyzed: https://www.cloudbeds.com/online-travel-agencies/commissions/). Run the arithmetic on a 20-room, $180-ADR property at 70% occupancy and that's roughly $135,000 a year — an illustrative model with stated assumptions, not a universal figure.

The infrastructure to fix this just got heavily funded: Mews raised $300M at a $2.5B valuation in January 2026, the largest round in hospitality software history (PR Newswire: https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mews-secures-300-million-investment-to-cement-position-as-worlds-leading-hospitality-operating-system-302668120.html). Cloudbeds has raised $250M including SoftBank and serves 27,000 properties.

This episode covers direct booking recovery: installing and running the rate-parity, booking-engine, missed-call, and past-guest re-book stack for independent hotels — priced against the commission saved, in a market where almost no provider publishes a price.

Full sources, the tool stack, and the build plan are in the blueprint linked below.

beats.vo_text: Independent hotels hand about two thirds of their bookings to Booking.com and Expedia, and pay 18 to 30 percent commission to do it. A 20-room hotel at 70 percent occupancy loses roughly $135,000 a year to that math.
beats.asset_hint: chart: booking split — 63% OTA vs 37% direct, with commission range 18-30% called out
beats.source: Cloudbeds 2026 State of Independent Hotels report (~90M bookings), https://www.cloudbeds.com/online-travel-agencies/commissions/; $135,000 figure is an illustrative arithmetic model, not a vendor-reported number

beats.vo_text: This is direct booking recovery: installing and running the stack that gets a hotel's own website booking rooms instead of Booking.com or Expedia doing it for a cut. Rate parity monitoring, a real booking engine, a missed-call system, and a re-book flow to past guests — the plumbing one person can run for a dozen properties at once.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'Direct Booking Recovery' + 4 bullets (parity, booking engine, missed-call, re-book)

beats.vo_text: It serves independent hotels in the ten-to-forty-room band — big enough that commission is real money, small enough that nobody on staff owns revenue management. Five years ago this required a channel-manager contract and a consultant on retainer. Now Mews, Cloudbeds, and SiteMinder run the parity checks, and a voice agent answers the phone the front desk can't get to.
beats.asset_hint: logo row: Mews, Cloudbeds, SiteMinder

beats.vo_text: Nobody on staff was watching that number, and it was not negligence. A small property leans on the OTAs for a reason: you do not have the manpower to take it all in, and you do not have the skillset to build direct. And direct booking is not a website. Build it and they will come is not true here. It is marketing — putting yourself out there, continuously. That is the job nobody had time for, and it is the job the agents are actually for. Not answering. Outreach, profile, follow-up. Your own growth engine rather than a better voicemail.
beats.asset_hint: broll: operator at laptop reviewing a booking dashboard, split-screen with a hotel exterior

beats.vo_text: Cloudbeds — who sell the software that fixes this — looked at ninety million bookings for their 2026 State of Independent Hotels report and found that independents lose 63.4 percent of reservations to OTAs. Once you add Booking.com's Genius program and Visibility Booster, or Expedia's Accelerator, the real commission runs 18 to 30 percent, well above the 15-to-25 headline rate hotels think they're paying.
beats.asset_hint: chart: headline OTA rate (15-25%) vs all-in rate with loyalty programs added (18-30%)
beats.source: Cloudbeds 2026 State of Independent Hotels report, https://www.cloudbeds.com/online-travel-agencies/commissions/ — vendor-published, attribute aloud

beats.vo_text: Same dataset: OTA bookings cancel at 21.8 percent, almost double the 10.6 percent for direct. The commission doesn't just cost money — it buys a less reliable booking. Run the arithmetic on a real property: 20 rooms, $180 average rate, 70 percent occupancy, books around $920,000 a year. Two thirds through OTAs at 22 percent all-in is about $135,000 gone to commission.
beats.asset_hint: slide: illustrative model — 20 rooms / $180 ADR / 70% occupancy / $135K commission, labeled 'estimate, assumptions stated'
beats.source: Cancellation rates: Cloudbeds 2026 report; $135,000 figure is an illustrative estimate built from those assumptions, not a company-reported number

beats.vo_text: At Coqui Coqui the first thing I did was get the brand and the site into good form. Then the harder part: making the whole flow hold together. Social to the website, the website to a call or a booking, the booking through to check-in — one continued conversation instead of four handoffs. I could do that because I had fifty people on property and the time to think about it. A B&B operator running the place alone cannot. That gap is the whole opportunity.
beats.asset_hint: broll: busy front-desk checkout queue, phone visibly ringing unanswered

beats.vo_text: On the high end, Mews just raised $300 million in a Series D led by EQT Growth, valuing the company at $2.5 billion — the largest funding round hospitality software has ever seen. Announced January 2026. New investors Atomico and HarbourVest joined existing backers Kinnevik, Battery Ventures, and Tiger Global.
beats.asset_hint: logo: Mews + slide: 'Series D — $300M — $2.5B valuation — Jan 2026'
beats.source: Mews press release via PR Newswire, https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/mews-secures-300-million-investment-to-cement-position-as-worlds-leading-hospitality-operating-system-302668120.html; Hotel Dive, https://www.hoteldive.com/news/mews-series-d-300-million-funding/810338/

beats.vo_text: Mews now moves $19.7 billion a year across 42 million bookings and 15,000 customers in 85 countries. Cloudbeds has raised $250 million, including SoftBank, and serves 27,000 properties. Mews earmarked this round for AI agents that automate hotel operations — but somebody still has to install that plumbing in a 20-room property that has never had a revenue manager.
beats.asset_hint: chart: Mews vs Cloudbeds scale — transaction volume, customer count, funding raised
beats.source: Mews figures: PR Newswire release + Hotel Dive (see prior beat); Cloudbeds figures: company reporting as compiled in research brief

beats.vo_text: The low end is thinner, and in the wrong unit. Freelance remote hotel revenue managers earn an average $129,482 a year, according to ZipRecruiter — that's a salary, not a price you charge a hotel. Senior independent consultants generally bill $400 to $700 an hour, with retainers discounted 10 to 15 percent — but that's a generic consulting benchmark, not one built for hotels.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'What this isn't' — salary figure crossed against a price tag icon
beats.source: ZipRecruiter, https://www.ziprecruiter.com/Jobs/Freelance-Remote-Hotel-Revenue-Management; consulting hourly range is a generic cross-industry benchmark, not hotel-specific, marked as estimate

beats.vo_text: Providers like TCRM, Revenuenaire, and HotelMinder claim 5 to 15 percent RevPAR uplift, but every one of them quotes privately — nobody in this market publishes a price. That's not a hole in the research. That's the finding: a market where nobody prices in public is a market a published price can walk straight into.
beats.asset_hint: slide: outsourced revenue-management providers listed with 'price: on request' stamped across each
beats.source: Reported vendor claims (TCRM, Revenuenaire, Catala, HotelMinder, MS Hospitality) — private pricing observed on each site; no public per-property rate found, mark as reported gap

beats.vo_text: The core is a property-management system with a real booking engine attached — Mews or Cloudbeds, both running partner programs worth checking before you build on them. For properties under about 30 rooms, Little Hotelier is the lighter, cheaper tier. This is what replaces the OTA's booking flow on the hotel's own site — the piece that actually captures the direct reservation instead of losing it to a search result.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: booking engine checkout flow on a hotel's own website

beats.vo_text: On top of that sits SiteMinder, the channel manager that keeps rates identical across every OTA and the hotel's own site — rate parity is where deals leak first, so a monitor watching for mismatches runs continuously, not on a schedule. This is the layer that stops a hotel from accidentally undercutting its own direct rate.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: rate-parity dashboard flagging a mismatch across OTAs

beats.vo_text: The phone is the same fix as episode two: Twilio underneath a voice agent that answers when the front desk can't, because a chunk of the bookings lost to OTAs never even got to a website — they were calls that rang out. Pair it with a simple booking widget, like Cal.com, so a caller who wants to book can just do it.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: voice agent call flow answering a missed call and booking a room

beats.vo_text: The last piece is the cheapest booking a hotel will ever get: a past guest. A basic email tool — Beehiiv or similar — runs the re-book flow, reminding people who already stayed once that they can book direct next time, no commission attached. It's unglamorous and it's where the highest-margin bookings actually come from.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: automated re-book email sequence in Beehiiv

beats.vo_text: All together, licensing this stack for one property runs a few hundred dollars a month — a rounding error against a $135,000 commission bill, which is the entire pitch.
beats.asset_hint: slide: stack cost (few hundred/mo) vs commission lost ($135K/yr) side by side
beats.source: Estimate: typical SMB PMS/channel-manager/voice-agent stack pricing; not itemized in research brief

beats.vo_text: Week one: pick five to ten independent hotels in the ten-to-forty-room band — big enough that commission is real money, small enough that nobody on staff owns this. Pull each one's OTA booking mix and run the commission arithmetic from the evidence section against their actual numbers. That number, not a pitch deck, is the sales call.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'Week 1' + checklist — pick properties, pull OTA mix, run the math

beats.vo_text: Be straight with the hotel about what this is and isn't: OTAs stay. They're distribution and discovery, not the enemy. The pitch isn't 'drop Booking.com' — it's shifting the mix, and shifting the mix by even ten points is real money at these margins.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'Not this: drop OTAs' crossed out / 'This: shift the mix' checked

beats.vo_text: Month one is the first signed property. Fix the leaks in the order they cost money: rate parity first, because a mismatched rate is actively pushing bookings to the OTA; then the booking engine itself; then the missed-call line, which is the direct callback to episode two; then the re-book flow to past guests. Each fix is visible in the numbers within weeks, not quarters.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'Month 1' fix order — parity, booking engine, missed-call, re-book

beats.vo_text: Price against the commission saved, not against hours worked — a hotel losing $135,000 a year will pay a fraction of that gladly. Then do the thing nobody else in this market does: publish the price. Every outsourced revenue-management provider checked for this episode — TCRM, Revenuenaire, Catala, HotelMinder — quotes privately. A number on a website, in a market with none, is itself the pitch.
beats.asset_hint: screen_rec: a simple pricing page for the service, publicly listed
beats.source: Reported vendor scan (TCRM, Revenuenaire, Catala, HotelMinder) — private pricing observed, no public rate found

beats.vo_text: Realistically the first dollar lands three to six weeks in, as soon as the first signed property's parity fix goes live and the direct-booking number starts moving.
beats.asset_hint: chart: direct-booking share ticking up in the weeks after the parity fix
beats.source: Estimate based on typical implementation timeline for rate-parity and booking-engine fixes; not itemized in research brief

beats.vo_text: After that it's one report a month: direct-booking share, before and after. That single number is what turns a first property into a referral, and a referral into the second, third, and fourth — the same local-density model as episode two, just with a bigger check attached.
beats.asset_hint: chart: month-over-month direct-booking share report, growing client count

beats.vo_text: The harder question isn't landing the first property — it's what happens at the tenth, when audits, parity fixes, and monthly reports for a dozen hotels are competing for the same week. Whether that scales as an agency or caps out as a solid side income is the next question.
beats.asset_hint: slide: single operator icon vs small-agency org chart, question mark between them

beats.vo_text: There's a full walkthrough of this audit, the pricing structure, and the outreach approach in the blueprint linked below, for anyone who'd rather start from a built checklist than piece one together.
beats.asset_hint: slide: blueprint cover mockup — 'Direct Booking Recovery: audit, pricing, outreach'

beats.vo_text: On effort, not promise: running the audit and fixes for three or four properties as a side operation is realistic supplemental income, closer to the freelance revenue-management range of roughly $95,000 to $140,000 a year for a full-time equivalent — not what any single hotel pays, but what the workload adds up to at ten or twelve clients.
beats.asset_hint: chart: income range by number of client properties (3-4 vs 10-12)
beats.source: ZipRecruiter freelance revenue-management salary range, https://www.ziprecruiter.com/Jobs/Freelance-Remote-Hotel-Revenue-Management, reframed as a full-time-equivalent workload estimate — this is salaried pay data, not a client rate

beats.vo_text: What it actually diversifies is skills and optionality more than a single income stream: revenue-management literacy, a channel-manager and voice-agent stack you can resell into other verticals, and a client roster that doesn't disappear if any one algorithm change wipes out a single OTA relationship.
beats.asset_hint: slide: three icons — revenue literacy, resellable stack, diversified client base

beats.vo_text: Costs stay real: software licenses run a few hundred dollars a month per property, and the failure mode is a hotel that signs, sees one good month, and doesn't renew because nobody proved the number moved. Whether the pricing model survives that renewal conversation is the actual test.
beats.asset_hint: slide: 'Failure mode' — one good month, no renewal, chart flatlining
beats.source: Estimate: cost and churn-risk reasoning based on typical SaaS/service retainer dynamics; not itemized in research brief

beats.vo_text: The full audit template, the pricing structure, and the outreach script are all in the direct-booking blueprint linked below — the same checklist used to build this episode. Subscribe for the next installment in this series: one person, one commission-heavy market, built out step by step.
beats.asset_hint: slide: blueprint + subscribe end card

blueprint_summary.idea: Install and operate the direct-booking recovery stack for independent hotels — rate parity, booking engine, missed-call recovery, and past-guest re-book flows — priced against the OTA commission saved instead of hours worked.
blueprint_summary.who_its_for: Independent hotel owners with roughly 10-40 rooms who have no in-house revenue manager and are losing an estimated 18-30% of two-thirds of their bookings to OTA commission.

tool_stack.role: PMS + booking engine — captures the direct reservation
Channel manager + rate-parity monitoring across OTAs
Lighter PMS tier for properties under ~30 rooms
Answers missed calls — the phone-side booking recovery, callback to episode two
Direct booking widget for the hotel's own site
Re-book email flow to past guests

blueprint_summary.first_customer_plan: Audit an independent hotel's OTA booking mix, compute its annual commission exposure using the property's real numbers, and use that figure as the sales pitch. Fix rate parity first — it's the fastest visible win — then the booking engine, missed-call line, and re-book flow. First dollar typically lands three to six weeks after signing.
blueprint_summary.realistic_economics: No public per-property price exists in this market, which is itself the opportunity. Running the stack for 10-12 client properties tracks toward the freelance revenue-management range of roughly $95,000-$140,000/year (ZipRecruiter) as a full-time equivalent — but that figure reflects salaried work, not a published client rate. Software costs run a few hundred dollars a month per property against commission exposure that can reach six figures annually for a single mid-size independent hotel.
